questions.explanation: Partial failure means the system is neither fully up nor fully down — some nodes keep running while others crash or are cut off, unlike a single machine where one crash stops everything. The distractors invert this: partial failures need not lose data or be permanent, and shutting down the whole cluster at once is the single-machine pattern, not the distributed one.
options: Part of the system keeps working while other parts fail, instead of everything halting at once
Partial failures always destroy data, while single-machine crashes never do
A partial failure shuts down the entire cluster simultaneously
Partial failures are always permanent, whereas crashes are always temporary
questions.question: What makes a partial failure different from a crash on a single computer?

questions.explanation: The book's contrast is philosophical: commodity/cloud infrastructure assumes components will fail and pushes resilience into software, while classic supercomputing assumed a reliable fabric and treated a failure as abort-and-retry the whole job. The distractors reverse the hardware story or claim faults can be eliminated — the chapter explicitly rejects that, since faults are unavoidable.
options: Supercomputers use commodity hardware while cloud systems rely on specialized interconnects

Cloud systems treat faults as routine and build tolerance into software; supercomputing traditionally assumed reliable interconnects and fail-stop behavior, aborting and retrying a failed job wholesale
Cloud systems never suffer hardware faults because redundancy eliminates them
Supercomputers tolerate partial failures gracefully while cloud systems crash entirely
questions.question: How does the book contrast cloud computing with supercomputing on handling faults?

questions.explanation: Loss, delay, duplication, link and switch failures, partitions, and congestion-driven buffer overflows are all routine in real networks. The last option describes a fantasy network — no real link offers instant, ordered, lossless delivery.
options: Packets lost, delayed, or duplicated in transit
Links or switches failing and splitting the network into partitions
Congestion filling switch buffers until packets are dropped
Every message arriving instantly and in order on all links
questions.question: Which of the following are realistic network faults you must design for? (select all that apply)

questions.explanation: A timeout cannot distinguish a dead node from a slow node, a dead link, a lost request, or a lost reply — all look identical to the sender. Concluding 'crashed' or 'never received' assumes knowledge you do not have; that unjustified leap is exactly the trap this section warns about.
options: The node has crashed
The request never reached the node
Nothing definitive — the node may be down, slow, or healthy with the reply lost or delayed
The network partition is permanent and will never heal
questions.question: You send a request to a node and receive no reply before your timeout expires. What can you safely conclude?

questions.explanation: Unbounded delay makes every timeout value a heuristic — too short and you get false failure alarms, too long and real failures go undetected for ages. And real networks are asynchronous: they promise no timing bound at all, so correct algorithms must not depend on one. TCP gives reliability with no latency bound, and retries can absolutely cause duplicate execution, which is why the other two options are wrong.
options: There is no dependable upper bound on message delay, so any timeout value is a guess: too short causes false failure alarms, too long delays real failure detection
Real networks are asynchronous — they offer no timing guarantees — so correct algorithms must not depend on bounded message delivery
TCP guarantees each message is delivered within a fixed, known deadline
Retrying a timed-out request is always safe because duplicate execution is impossible
questions.question: Which statements correctly describe timeouts and timing assumptions in real networks? (select all that apply)

questions.explanation: Measuring elapsed time needs a clock that never moves backward, and only monotonic clocks qualify. Wall clocks can jump backward on NTP adjustments or leap seconds, and cross-machine synchronization does not fix that. CPU cycle counters are a red herring — they are not stable or comparable across cores and frequency changes.
options: The time-of-day (wall) clock, because it is synchronized across machines
A monotonic clock, because it only moves forward — wall clocks can jump backward after NTP corrections or leap seconds
Either one; both always agree and neither ever moves backward
The CPU cycle counter, because wall clocks tick too slowly to be useful
questions.question: You need to measure how long an operation took. Which clock should you use, and why?

questions.explanation: NTP only bounds clock disagreement approximately — using UTC does not remove skew, and leap seconds actually break monotonicity by making clocks repeat or jump. With skew in play, a 'later' timestamp does not mean a later event, which is why last-write-wins can silently discard the truly-later write.
options: NTP keeps clocks close but some unknown offset always remains, so cross-machine timestamps cannot establish exact order
If every node uses UTC, timestamp order is guaranteed to match the real order of events
Clock skew can stamp an earlier event with a 'later' time, so last-write-wins can silently discard the truly-later write
Leap seconds make wall clocks strictly monotonic
questions.question: Which statements are true about using timestamps from different machines to order events? (select all that apply)

questions.explanation: A pause freezes a node without killing it, so it resumes with outdated beliefs — the classic hazard is a deposed leader issuing writes as if it were still in charge (which is why fencing tokens exist). Pauses do not wipe memory or corrupt clocks, and they can strike any node, leader included.
options: The paused process loses all of its in-memory state
A paused leader can wake up believing it still leads and act on stale authority after being deposed
Pauses permanently corrupt the process's clock beyond repair
Pauses only ever affect follower nodes, never leaders
questions.question: What danger do process pauses — e.g., stop-the-world garbage collection or VM suspension — create in a leader-based system?

questions.explanation: The interval is honest about uncertainty — it never shrinks to zero — and the commit-wait delays the commit until it is certain the timestamp has passed in real time. Trusting the midpoint or disabling NTP pretends the uncertainty away, which is exactly what this section warns against.
options: Waiting out the clock uncertainty before committing, so the assigned timestamp order is safe
Retrying the clock read until the interval shrinks to zero
Trusting the midpoint of the interval as the exact time
Disabling NTP on the committing node during the transaction
questions.question: Spanner copes with uncertain clocks by treating each reading as a confidence interval [earliest, latest] and then…

questions.explanation: A partitioned node cannot tell whether it or the others failed — asking over the broken network is circular, and there is no 'oldest node' oracle. The standard resolution defines truth by majority: the side that cannot assemble a quorum stands down, preventing split-brain. Staying available on both sides is precisely the failure this avoids.
options: It should keep serving requests to stay available
It should ask the other nodes over the network who is at fault
It applies majority rule: if it cannot reach a quorum, it assumes it is the faulty side and stops acting
The oldest node in the cluster always decides which side is correct
questions.question: A network partition isolates one node from the rest of the cluster. How should the isolated node decide whether it is the faulty side?

questions.explanation: Fencing tokens guard resources against stale holders that were paused rather than dead; Byzantine faults mean arbitrary or malicious behavior and are far costlier to tolerate than crash faults, which is why most systems do not attempt it; and weaker 'lying' happens without malice, like reporting durability for data still sitting in a cache. Correctness is always relative to the assumed system model, and safety (nothing bad happens) is a different property from liveness (something good eventually happens). The last option is wrong on both counts: most systems assume crash faults, and crash faults absolutely do occur.
options: Each lock grant carries a monotonically increasing fencing token, and the resource rejects writes with a token older than the newest one seen — protecting against a stale holder that was merely paused, not dead

Byzantine faults cover arbitrary behavior including lying or malicious acts, cost far more to tolerate than crash faults, and most systems do not attempt it; weaker lying happens without malice, like claiming durability for data still sitting in a cache

An algorithm is correct only under its system model (timing assumptions crossed with failure assumptions); safety means nothing bad ever happens and liveness means something good eventually happens — they are distinct properties
Most databases assume Byzantine faults by default because crash faults never occur in practice
questions.question: Which statements about fencing, Byzantine faults, and system models are correct? (select all that apply)

questions.explanation: The chapter's thesis is to design for faults as the norm and to treat every timing or knowledge assumption — timeouts, timestamps, failure detection — as suspect rather than factual. Redundancy reduces but never eliminates partial failure, and the chapter argues the opposite about clocks: NTP does not make timestamps safe for ordering events.
options: Expect partial failures, unreliable networks, and unreliable clocks — design software that behaves correctly under them instead of assuming them away
Every timing or knowledge assumption your design depends on — bounded delays, accurate clocks, 'that node is dead' — is a potential failure mode and must be handled, not taken as fact
With enough redundancy, partial failures can be eliminated entirely
The chapter concludes that synchronized clocks are safe for ordering events as long as you run NTP
questions.question: Which statements capture this chapter's overall lessons? (select all that apply)

summary.overview: This chapter is about why distributed systems are fundamentally harder than single-machine programs: failures are partial rather than total, networks drop and delay messages with no upper bound, clocks disagree and jump, and no node can reliably tell what is true about the rest of the system. It matters because every fault-tolerance mechanism in the chapters that follow — replication, partitioning, consensus — is built on top of these realities, and misjudging them (trusting a timeout, a timestamp, or a failure detector) is a classic source of real-world outages.

sections.heading: Faults and Partial Failures
takeaways: Failures in distributed systems are partial: some nodes keep running while others crash or become unreachable — unlike a single computer, where one crash stops everything at once.
This partial failure is what makes distributed programming fundamentally different from single-machine programming: your code must decide how to behave when only part of the system is reachable.

Cloud-style systems built from commodity hardware treat faults as routine and push fault tolerance into software; supercomputing-style systems historically assumed reliable, low-latency interconnects and fail-stop behavior, aborting and retrying a failed job wholesale.
Hardware faults — dead disks, crashed machines, dropped links — are unavoidable, so behaving correctly during faults is a core design requirement, not a rare edge case.

sections.heading: Unreliable Networks
takeaways: Network faults are routine: packets are lost, delayed, or duplicated; links, switches, and NICs fail; partitions split the network.
A missing reply is ambiguous — you cannot reliably tell a crashed node apart from a slow node or a broken link, so timeout-based failure detection is always a guess.
There is no dependable upper bound on message delay: short timeouts cause false failure alarms, long timeouts delay real failure detection, and retries risk executing a request twice.
Congestion causes queueing: when switch buffers fill up, packets are dropped — overload turns into delay and loss.
Real networks are asynchronous (no timing guarantees); correct algorithms must not depend on bounded message delivery, because the synchronous model does not hold in practice.

sections.heading: Unreliable Clocks
takeaways: Time-of-day (wall) clocks can jump backward — NTP corrections, leap seconds, manual changes — so measure elapsed time and timeouts with a monotonic clock, which only moves forward.
Clock synchronization via NTP is only approximate: machines always disagree by some unknown offset, so timestamps from different nodes cannot establish exact event order.
Ordering events by timestamp (e.g. last-write-wins) can silently lose data: clock skew can stamp the earlier event with the 'later' time.
Clock uncertainty can be made explicit as a confidence interval [earliest, latest]; Spanner waits out that uncertainty before committing so timestamp order stays safe.
Process pauses — stop-the-world GC, VM suspension or migration, OS descheduling — can freeze a node that wakes up believing stale state, such as a leader that was deposed while paused.

sections.heading: Knowledge, Truth, and Lies
takeaways: A node cut off by a partition cannot tell whether it or the others are faulty; the standard fix is majority rule — a side that cannot reach a quorum assumes it is the faulty one and stops acting.
Fencing tokens protect shared resources from stale lock holders: each lock grant carries an increasing token, and the resource rejects writes carrying a token older than the newest one it has seen.

Byzantine faults mean arbitrary behavior — including lying or malicious acts — and cost far more to tolerate than crash faults, so most systems do not try; weaker lying happens without malice, e.g. claiming a write is durable while it is still in a cache, or corruption slipping past checksums.

Every algorithm is correct only under its system model — its timing assumptions (synchronous, partially synchronous, asynchronous) crossed with its failure assumptions (crash-stop, crash-recovery, Byzantine); safety ('nothing bad ever happens') and liveness ('something good eventually happens') are separate properties, and breaking the model's assumptions breaks the guarantees.

sections.heading: Summary
takeaways: The chapter's core lesson: expect partial failures, unreliable networks, and unreliable clocks — design software that behaves correctly under them instead of assuming them away.
Treat every timing or knowledge assumption your design depends on — bounded delays, accurate clocks, 'that node is dead' — as a potential failure mode, not a fact.
